validated_results.title: Association of Artificially Sweetened Beverage Consumption and Urinary Tract Cancers in the Women's Health Initiative Observational Study.
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of postmenopausal women reporting adjusted hazard ratio for incident kidney cancer by artificially sweetened beverage consumption.

extraction.comparison_type: Frequent consumption (one to six servings per week) vs rare consumption
extraction.timing: Baseline consumption assessed 1993-1998 with mean follow-up of 13.5 yr to February 28, 2020
extraction.population: Postmenopausal women aged 50-79 yr in the Women's Health Initiative Observational Study

sample_size.excerpt: We identified 80 388 participants who met the inclusion criteria.

effect_size.excerpt: Cox regression models showed that frequent artificially sweetened beverage consumption was associated with a higher risk of kidney cancer (adjusted hazard ratio 1.34, 95% confidence interval 1.03-1.75).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Cox regression models showed that frequent artificially sweetened beverage consumption was associated with a higher risk of kidney cancer (adjusted hazard ratio 1.34, 95% confidence interval 1.03-1.75).

comparison.excerpt: rare artificially sweetened beverage consumption (never to fewer than one serving per week), frequent consumption (one to six servings per week), and daily consumption (more than one servings per day)

design.excerpt: a multicenter longitudinal prospective study of the health of 93 676 postmenopausal women

continent.excerpt: Women were identified at 40 clinical centers across the USA

exposure_measurement.excerpt: We included women who answered questions about artificially sweetened beverage consumption

extraction.p_value_method: two-sided Wald test from effect and 95% CI on the log scale
extraction.ethnicity_basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available

parallel_r3_gate_reasons: important quantitative evidence remains missing or invalid: cases
